messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mai, a 57-year-old married midwife, had built her life around keeping other women safe in moments that were often private, painful, and intimate. She described the rape as having happened years earlier, after an evening shift when she was walking home and a man she had passed several times in her neighborhood followed her into a dim passageway. What stayed with her was not only the assault itself but the smell of burnt oil from a nearby food stall, drifting into the narrow space as she was pinned and unable to get away; even now, that smell could make her stomach lurch before she understood why. In the weeks after, she noticed that simply feeling uncomfortable in a room, or noticing that people were looking at her, could pull her back into a sense that something bad was about to happen. She had come to believe that if she felt exposed, if someone’s eyes lingered on her in the wrong way, she might be in danger again, and she began watching herself through other people’s gaze.

Over time, Mai’s attention narrowed onto signs that others might pose a threat. At home she listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering the house, lying awake after her husband had fallen asleep, rigidly tracking the settling noises of the building and every footfall outside the front door. In public and at work she studied people’s faces and body language, reading for the slightest shift in posture, a too-direct look, a closed jaw, anything that might signal intent. She did this instinctively with patients’ relatives at the clinic, but also in the market, on the bus, and in the corridor outside the apartment where she lived. What frightened her most was how quickly her body reacted when something reminded her of the assault: her heart would pound, her skin would go hot, and she would feel as if she had been caught off guard all over again. Those reactions made her even more certain that danger was close, because she interpreted the rush in her body as proof that she had missed some warning sign.

That sense of threat then began to feed the very things that set it off. The more Mai felt unsafe, the more uncomfortable she became in ordinary situations that required her to be noticed. She found herself avoiding eye contact with neighbors and shrinking when clients looked directly at her in the maternity ward, where she had spent decades moving with calm authority. Being seen, especially when she was tired or alone, made her feel exposed rather than visible, and she increasingly chose routes and routines that let her stay on the edge of attention. At home, any burnt smell—from cooking oil left too long on the stove, from an overheated pan in a neighbor’s kitchen—could make her tense and scan the apartment, and if she caught that odor in the hospital staff room she would step out quickly, saying little, as though lingering might invite something worse. These moments did not stay isolated. Once her body had spiked with alarm, she would spend the rest of the day on guard, checking faces more closely, listening harder at night, and bracing for the next reminder. The more she monitored for danger, the more easily she found it, and the more strongly she reacted when it appeared.

In recent months this pattern had begun to wear down the life she had carefully maintained. Mai slept lightly, woke to small noises, and felt drained by the effort of staying alert in a house she had once experienced as safe. At work she remained competent, but she felt increasingly detached from the warm, steady role she valued, and she had started to decline some late appointments because the walk home afterward felt intolerable. Her husband noticed that she was quieter and less willing to join neighbors, though she brushed off his concern with practical explanations. What finally brought her to seek help was a particularly bad evening when the smell of something burning in the building’s corridor, followed by footsteps on the stairs, sent her heart racing and left her trembling for hours. She told the therapist that she was frightened of becoming “like this forever,” always listening, always scanning faces, always startled in her own life, but she also hoped that if she understood why her body kept reacting so intensely, she might be able to step back into the world without feeling hunted by it.
